result:
The final answer is in `final.py` (a copy of c14). It finds exactly the same pairs as the reference and scores about **91–97× on the search split**. I used **15 of the 24 scorer calls** and about 12 minutes of the default 15-minute budget.

| | search score (scorer) | my unseen test seeds |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | ≈1.0 | 1.0 |
| first champion (c1) | 76.3 | ~38–45× |
| **final (c14)** | **91.5, 90.8; 97.1 on the confirm run** | **48×** |

The 97.1 is partly luck: the reference happened to run slower on that pass (1.42 s against the usual 1.33 s), so ~91 is the honest figure. I could not do the held-out scoring step, because `./score` only covers the search split. In its place I used test seeds on my own generator that I never tuned on. All 5 matched the reference exactly at 48×.

**Why it's faster.** The reference compares every pair of records. The final version only compares records that could possibly reach 80%:
- **Size filter:** a record of n words can only match one with at least 0.8·n words, so smaller records are skipped. Records are handled in size order, which lets the index drop records that have become too small.
- **Shared-rare-word filter:** each record's words are sorted rarest-first. Two records can only reach 80% if one shares a word with the first few rarest words of the other, so only those few words are looked up in an index.
- **Exact check:** each remaining candidate is checked with the same integer test as the specification (9·|A∩B| ≥ 4·(|A|+|B|)).
- **Shortcut for records of 1–4 words:** the size rule forces the same size, and 80% then means identical word sets. So these are just grouped by identical sets. 4-word records are still indexed so 5-word records can find them.

**Approaches tried and how each did on the scorer:**

| approach | score | kept? |
|---|---|---|
| rare-word filter, first version (c1) | 76 | became the starting point |
| extra filter on word positions to cut candidates (c4) | 75 | dropped |
| group identical records first (c7) | 74 | dropped |
| order words by first appearance instead of counting them (c8, c13) | ties | dropped: worse on my tests, and less reliable on new inputs |
| skip words that appear only once (c10) | 67 | dropped |
| leaner version of c1 (c11) | 85.5, 82.2 | parent of c12 |
| leaner version with a special case for 1–4 word records (c12) | 87.5, 90.2 | parent of c14 |
| look up "one word removed" subsets for 5–8 word records (c15) | 80.8 | dropped |
| further tightening of c14 (c16) | 91.9 | dropped: a tie, so I kept the simpler c14 |

**Things to know:**
- My local test data ranked candidates differently from the scorer, so I chose on scorer results and used the local tests only to check correctness.
- On inputs built to be worst cases, the speed-up disappears but stays well inside the 3× cutoff. When every record is identical it runs at the reference's speed, because the answer itself has over a million pairs. With long records drawn from a small vocabulary it is also about the reference's speed. With a tiny vocabulary it is about 2.7× faster.
- Two Claude Docs connectors (Atlassian Rovo, HyperFrames by HeyGen) need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. This task did not need them.

**Candidate log** (calls left: 9):
```
c1  set-union of prefix postings, size filter   76.3   champion 1
c4  + positional filter                         75.4   dropped
c7  identical-set grouping + c4                 74.2   dropped
c8  c7, first-seen word order                   74.3   dropped
c10 singleton-token skip                        67.1   dropped
c11 lean c1 (map/frozenset, buckets, key sort)  85.5, 82.2
c12 c11 + min() for 1-token prefix              87.5, 90.2
c13 c12, first-seen word order                  88.2   tie, less robust, dropped
c14 c12 + identical-only shortcut for n<=4      91.5, 90.8  FINAL
c15 subset lookup for n=5..8                    80.8   dropped
c16 c14 general-branch tightening               91.9   tie, dropped
final.py (= c14) confirm                        97.1
```
